title: Removing a Nested Contributor requires a SKY holder vote in addition to a GROVE holder vote for three years after genesis
content:
A.6.1.1.2.2.2.2.2.1.2.1.6.1 imposes a time-boxed supermajority-of-constituencies rule: "For a period of three years after the Genesis Supply emissions of GROVE tokens take place, any Artifact Edit that would have the effect of removing a Nested Contributor must be approved by a vote of SKY holders in addition to a vote of GROVE holders to be effective."

The drafting is deliberately effects-based — "would have the effect of removing" — which closes the obvious workaround of achieving removal indirectly by stripping the contributor's role, budget or access rather than naming it.

What the provision buys is **credible commitment to the builders**. A development company will not invest years of work into an Agent whose token holders can eject it the moment the product is valuable. Requiring two electorates to agree makes ejection expensive and slow, so the contributor can plan on a multi-year horizon.

What it costs is Grove's autonomy over its own core supplier during exactly the period when performance problems are most likely to surface. If the Nested Contributor underperforms in year one, GROVE holders can vote to remove it and still be overruled by SKY holders — who, holding 70% of GROVE's genesis supply, have their own stake in continuity.

Read alongside the submission-threshold exemption (A.6.1.1.2.2.2.2.2.1.2.1.1.1), the Nested Contributor category is privileged at both ends: easiest to initiate governance, hardest to remove.
description: During the entrenchment window Grove's own token holders cannot unilaterally sever the Nested Contributor; Sky must concur, protecting the development company from the Agent's own governance.
